name: Square Kauri

location.address: Square Kauri Track, Tapu-Coroglen Road, Coromandel Forest Park, Coromandel Peninsula, New Zealand
location.neighbourhood: Coromandel Forest Park, 8.5 km from Tapu

access: Free. DOC-maintained track directly off the Tapu-Coroglen Road, a public road across the Coromandel Range between Tapu and Coroglen. Short but steep, 187 steps, about 2-3 minutes each way. No gate, no ticket.
transport: No public transport; reached by car on the Tapu-Coroglen Road, roughly 8.5 km from the settlement of Tapu on the Coromandel's west coast.
story:
The loggers who took almost every big kauri off the Coromandel left this one standing because it was the wrong shape. Its trunk is squared off, angular where a kauri should be round, and to a nineteenth-century timber trade that made it commercially useless. The rest of the peninsula's giants went to the mills. This one stayed, saved by the very feature that now makes it a landmark.

It is not the biggest kauri on the Coromandel. By volume it ranks about fifteenth. Measured in 1975, the trunk was 8.76 metres round and held close to 70 cubic metres of wood, and the tree stands a little over 41 metres tall. Its age is usually given as around 1,200 years, a round figure the sources repeat rather than a count anyone has made, so read it as somewhere past a thousand.

What it has that the bigger trees do not is a name, a silhouette you will not confuse with anything else, and a place right on the road. The Department of Conservation keeps a short track to it off the Tapu-Coroglen Road, which crosses the Coromandel Range between the two coasts: 187 steep steps up from the roadside, two or three minutes each way, no gate and no ticket.

It is a good place to think about how many old trees are still standing because somebody once decided they were not worth the trouble.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, squared off at the edges rather than round, 8.76 metres in girth. It stands at the top of the 187-step track off the Tapu-Coroglen Road.

name: McKinney Kauri

location.address: Parry Kauri Park, Tudor Collins Drive, Warkworth, Auckland, New Zealand (beside the Warkworth & District Museum)

access: Free. Auckland Council public park with a boardwalk loop (about 20-35 minutes, partly wheelchair accessible), reached from a free car park at the Warkworth & District Museum on Tudor Collins Drive. Car park open 7am-9pm in summer, 7am-7pm in winter. Kauri dieback cleaning stations at the entrance; visitors asked to stay on the boardwalk.
transport: In Warkworth town centre, adjoining the museum; a short walk from central Warkworth. No public transport check done; reached easily by car off SH1, about an hour north of Auckland.
story:
The biggest kauri on New Zealand's east coast stands beside a museum car park in Warkworth. That is the claim the Warkworth museum makes for it, and the local tourism office and the trail guides repeat it: a trunk more than seven metres round, measured at 7.62, on a tree about 38 metres tall and roughly 800 years old. "Probably the largest", one of them adds, which is the honest way to hold a title nobody has formally settled.

It is still here because of a fundraiser. The park is the old property of the Reverend McKinney, later the Simpson family's, and the two giants at its entrance carry those two names. About fifty years ago the Warkworth Kauri Bushmen's Association raised money for one purpose, to save these two trees, and gave the land to the council once it was secured. Everything around them is what that fundraising bought.

Today the McKinney Kauri rises straight out of mown grass, a single clean trunk with a fence around its base and its crown still full and healthy. A boardwalk loop runs on into the bush behind it, 20 to 35 minutes if you walk the whole thing, and part of it takes a wheelchair.

Two requests come with the visit, and both are for the tree. Scrub your shoes at the cleaning station on the way in, because kauri dieback travels in soil. And stay on the boards.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the girth, more than seven metres round, the thicker of the two kauri at the park entrance, standing alone in mown grass with a fence around its base. It stands beside the Warkworth Museum car park.

name: Simpson Kauri
age_estimate: 600 years, per the tree's own on-site plaque

location.address: Parry Kauri Park, Tudor Collins Drive, Warkworth, Auckland, New Zealand (beside the Warkworth & District Museum, a few steps from the McKinney Kauri)

access: Same as McKinney Kauri: free Auckland Council park, boardwalk loop from the Warkworth Museum car park, cleaning stations for kauri dieback.
transport: Same as McKinney Kauri: in Warkworth town centre.
story:
The plaque on the Simpson Kauri gives away its own arithmetic: 5.79 metres round, 14.94 metres to the first limb, an estimated 30.6 cubic metres of wood, and an age of 600 years, four figures fixed to a bronze plate a few steps from a much bigger tree. That bigger tree is the McKinney Kauri, and the two of them stand together at the entrance to Parry Kauri Park because that is specifically what was saved.

Fifty years ago the land belonged to the Simpson family, before that to the Reverend McKinney, and the Warkworth Kauri Bushmen's Association raised money for exactly two trees rather than the whole property. Once the ground was secured it passed to Auckland Council, and that fundraiser is the only reason either kauri, or this park, still exists.

The Simpson Kauri is the quieter half of the pair, smaller than its neighbour by two metres of girth, and its 600-year age is the figure everyone repeats because the plaque is the only place it has ever been published. What the plaque actually measured is the trunk beneath the crown, nearly 15 metres of clean wood before the first limb, which is the number worth remembering it by.

A boardwalk keeps both trees' roots free of foot traffic, and cleaning stations at the entrance ask visitors to scrub kauri dieback off their shoes before they get near either one.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its bronze plaque, the second and slightly smaller of the two kauri at the Parry Kauri Park entrance, a few steps from the thicker McKinney Kauri.

name: Moko

location.address: Otari-Wilton's Bush, 150 Wilton Road, Wilton, Wellington, New Zealand (track starts at the Troup Picnic Lawn)

access: Free, open all hours, no ticket. Otari-Wilton's Bush is a Wellington City Council native botanic garden and forest reserve; main entrance and car park at 150 Wilton Road. A 20-30 minute track (a gentler zig-zag route opened 2022) leads from the Troup Picnic Lawn to a protective viewing platform built around the tree's roots.
transport: Number 14 (Wilton) bus from central Wellington; about 15 minutes by car from the city centre. Walking/biking also possible; bikes not permitted on the trails themselves.
story:
Wellington's oldest tree survived because an architect went to court for it. Decades before Otari-Wilton's Bush became the protected forest reserve it is today, Bob Fantl, a Bauhaus-trained architect and early environmentalist, fought to stop this rimu being felled, and the reason it still stands over Wilton Road is that he won.

It is a rimu rather than a kauri and carries none of a kauri's bulk: a trunk measured at 177.6 centimetres across in 2010, a height of 27.3 metres, its bark hung with epiphytes and perching lilies the way old-growth rimu usually are. Its age, repeated everywhere as about 800 years, is old enough that locals had already taken to calling it Wellington's oldest and tallest tree long before it had a name of its own.

It got one in July 2021, when local iwi gifted it the name Moko in a Matariki ceremony. In 2024 it was named a finalist for the country's Tree of the Year, decades after a single court case was the only thing standing between it and a saw.

A protective viewing platform now stands over its roots, reached by a 20 to 30 minute track from the Troup Picnic Lawn, rebuilt as a gentler zig-zag route in 2022 so the climb there does not itself become more foot traffic over the ground the tree needs.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the protective platform built around its roots at the end of the track, its trunk hung with epiphytes and perching lilies, Wellington's tallest tree.
